5 of the Quirkiest Engines the Volkswagen Group Ever Produced at the Orders of Ferdinand Piech
31 photos
Photo: Volkswagen AG
There was a time, only a few decades ago, when the Volkswagen Group was not only in a much better place than it is currently heading, but was arguably on its highest roll to date.
Not exactly a coincidence, that era started in 1993, when Ferdinand Piech became Chairman of the Group and immediately started a revolution that completely transformed the company. What followed across the next 22 years was a period of automotive engineering shenanigans that have never been repeated in Wolfsburg, and they probably never will.
I say this because the context in which it happened was simply unique. Ferdinand Piech was a genius engineer in complete control of a company with almost unlimited resources, and shareholders quickly learned that it was more fruitful to let him make whatever he wanted instead of arguing with him.
The total trust in him didn’t come immediately, but following a short period in which Piech’s managerial and engineering decisions upgraded the VW Group from the brink of bankruptcy to an automotive giant in almost no time. In 1993, VW lost approximately $1.1 billion USD due to soaring production costs, a drop in European sales and an inefficient cost structure.
The company was facing severe financial strain and was considered on the brink of bankruptcy due to soaring production costs, a drop in European volume markets, and inefficient management. Becoming the head honcho during the crisis prompted Piech to launch a massive restructuring effort that returned the group to profitability by the following year.
With the financial status becoming secure, Ferdinand slowly started to show his true motives for running the VW Group, with the main one being his dream of transforming it into the number one car company on the planet. He stopped short of usurping Toyota and General Motors, but during his tenure he did transform VW from a regional European carmaker into a global multi-brand empire, adding a number of highly coveted luxury brands to its roster and creating some of the coolest cars in the process.
For his contributions, he was named “Car Executive of the Century” in 1999, and his job at VW was only half done. Among the many changes Piech made to the company, he also introduced a number of innovations in Wolfsburg, including pioneering a standardized modular platform strategy across the entire group, and accepting no compromises regarding product quality.
A trained engineer by trade, he also became known for putting a lot of resources into expensive vanity projects , like the luxurious Volkswagen Phaeton or the mind-boggling Bugatti Veyron, and also for introducing a number of quirky engines that only cars from the Volkswagen Group used. This engineering excess was seen in almost every brand of the empire he had created, including under the hoods of cars that didn’t really need it.
With that in mind, I decided to curate a list of some of the most eccentric powertrains that Piech was personally responsible for being created and used. Most of them were commercial disasters, but all of them were magnificent for one reason or another, and none of them should be forgotten.
Volkswagen Beetle RSI: The Limited-Edition V6 Hot-Hatch that Wasn’t a V6 Launched in 1998, the retro-looking New Beetle was heavily inspired by the original Volkswagen Beetle when it comes to its exterior, while its architecture was completely switched around. Thanks to it using the VW Golf Mk IV’s platform, it was FWD with a transverse engine in the front instead of RWD with the engine in the rear, like the original.
In short, it was designed to be charming and invoke an emotional association with the first Beetle, especially the ones sold in the 1960s during the “Flower Power” movement, which is why each one came with a tiny flower vase in the dashboard. The New Beetle wasn’t designed to be practical, or fast, for that matter, but more as a lifestyle vehicle. Its most powerful engine in the beginning was a naturally aspirated, 2.3-liter five-cylinder with 170 PS (168 HP) that was quirky in its own right by being a V5, or VR5 as VW called it.
Photo: Volkswagen AG Its place at the top of the food chain was taken by a 3.2-liter VR6, which powered no more than 250 units of the Beetle RSI, launched in 2001 as the coolest version of the New Beetle, by far. Some would say that its $100k+ price and its motorsport-inspired looks were its most important attributes, but there are plenty others who became completely infatuated with its now legendary engine.
Especially for 2001, the engineering under the hood was simply extraordinary. The RSi debuted the 3.2-liter VR6 with four valves per cylinder, a naturally aspirated V6 that had more things in common with an inline-six cylinder engine than a V-angled one. This was not the first narrow-angle V6 made by VW , but it was the first one to debut the upcoming 24-valve 3.2-liter family of such engines, some of which would even arrive under the hoods of Porsches, not to mention the glorious Golf R32.
From some perspectives, the limited-edition Beetle RSI was more of a test bed for the engine, and despite “only” delivering 224 PS (221 HP), it used many motorsport-derived features that made it unique, even compared to the more powerful versions that followed. It came from the factory with a massive carbon fiber intake airbox to optimize airflow and boost induction sounds, and had a dual-exit exhaust system tuned by Austrian manufacturer Remus. To squeeze the wider block and a Haldex-based AWD system into the tight Beetle engine bay, there was no room for air conditioning routing, and the car famously even relied on manual window cranks to save weight.
Volkswagen Passat W8: The Only Production W8 Engine Ever Built Powered a Family Sedan Like with the Beetle RSI and its V6 with a 15-degree angle, the question of why the Volkswagen Passat W8 existed in the first place has both a simple answer and a complicated one. Believe it or not, both those answers are related to Ferdinand Piech, and both need the appropriate context.
Coincidentally, it was also unveiled in 2001, alongside the mid-cycle facelift for the B5 generation Volkswagen Passat, and its engine had more than one thing in common with the VR6 in the Beetle RSI. To create the peculiar 4.0-liter W8, Piech instructed VW engineers to make use of the modular concept from the EA390 VR6 family.
Photo: Volkswagen AG This is how, instead of a traditional 90-degree V8, with four cylinders on each side, the W8 practically consisted of two 15-degree VR4 engine blocks mounted onto a single, shared crankshaft at a 72-degree angle. This unique packaging solution made it incredibly compact for an 8-cylinder, measuring just 420 mm (16.5 in) in length, which is why it had no problem being fitted longitudinally under the hood of the B5.5 Passat, which could normally only house inline-fours and V6s at the most.
Again resembling the Beetle RSI, the Passat W8 was never intended to be a volume seller, with Piech deciding to make it as a test bed for the modular “W” engine concept that was about to take over many other brands of the VW Group, including Bentley and Bugatti. From that perspective, it’s no wonder fans of the model consider it “half a Bugatti engine.”
Unfortunately, the compact design and tight packaging came with some disadvantages as well, not to mention that it wasn’t exactly a pillar of performance with 275 PS (271 HP) from its 4.0-liter displacement. Maintenance costs were extremely high, as fixing basic elements from the rear of the engine sometimes required completely pulling the engine out of the car. Roughly 11,000 units in both sedan and station wagon guise were ever built, and no other production car in history has ever used a W8.
Volkswagen Touareg W12: The World’s First Unibody Twelve-Cylinder SUV The Volkswagen Touareg, as you all know, was developed jointly with Porsche, sharing its platform with the Cayenne and later with the Audi Q7, with the Bentley Bentayga and the Lamborghini Urus being created on the same underpinnings as well. From the beginning, it followed an entirely different recipe compared to its platform brothers, and it wasn’t supposed to go overboard with its engine lineup’s power range.
But then, someone at Volkswagen, with most of the fingers pointing, again, at Prof. Dr. techn. h.c. Dipl.-Ing. Ferdinand Karl Piech, decided that the Volkswagen Touareg needed a twelve-cylinder engine. That engine was the same 6.0-liter W12 developed for the Phaeton, which had already debuted on the Audi A8 and the Bentley Continental Flying Spur.
Photo: Volkswagen AG The powertrain had first appeared in various forms on a series of mid-engine supercar concepts, starting as early as the Giugiaro-penned 1997 Volkswagen W12 Syncro and ending with the record-breaking 2001 Nardo prototype. The Touareg W12 was only the world’s second-ever production SUV to feature a twelve-cylinder engine after the Lamborghini LM002 from the 1980s, also known as the “Rambo Lambo.” Coincidentally, Lamborghini was already part of the VW umbrella when the Touareg W12 entered production.
Initially, the model was supposed to be a limited-edition model, with just 500 units planned to be produced, 330 of which dedicated to the Saudi Arabia market. Eventually, the Touareg W12 became a production model and the halo version of the first-generation Touareg lineup. Naturally aspirated, it used a similar engine architecture as the Passat W8, with VW engineers fusing two banks of the same VR6 that debuted on the Beetle RSI together, and this gave it a length so short that it fit longitudinally without issues under the Touareg’s hood.
The downright insane idea that such a car should even exist as a production model was all thanks to Piech’s dreams of excessive engineering, which dominated most of the VW products during his tenure. Like the Beetle RSI and the Passat W8, the twelve-cylinder Touareg was not a commercial success, but that didn’t stop Ferdinand Porsche’s grandson from pushing for its existence.
Volkswagen Touareg V10 TDI: The Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde of Diesel SUVs Part of Ferdinand Piech’s master plan of upgrading the Volkswagen brand from a maker of “people’s cars” to a more premium one that could even go head to head with BMW and Mercedes-Benz required both new cars, like the Phaeton and Touareg, but also new technologies for its powertrains. One such technology was the proprietary “Pumpe Düse” technology for its diesel engines, which VW wanted to market against the competing Common Rail injection system.
For that marketing to work, Piech had the extravagant idea to create a halo diesel engine using the Pumpe Duse system, and this is pretty much how the V10 TDI came into existence, with the Touareg and the Phaeton being the first cars to be powered by it. From an engineering standpoint, the engine was not designed from scratch, making use of the modular technology that had also been used on the Passat W8 or the Touareg W12.
Photo: Volkswagen AG In essence, the V10 TDI effectively consisted of two 2.5-liter, inline-5 TDI engines fused together at a 90-degree angle. Therefore, the 2.5-liter R5 TDI and the V10 TDI shared the same cylinder bores and piston strokes, cylinder spacing and connecting rods.
Because it was structurally designed as two merged engines, the resulting 5.0-liter V10 also came with a number of engineering quirks, one of the most important being that it functioned using two of everything, including two separate engine control units (ECUs), two individual throttle bodies, two fuel pumps, and two mass airflow sensors.
This peculiarity was made even more obvious when you plugged a diagnostic scanner to it and the powertrain registered itself as being two distinct inline-5 engines. The 313 PS (309 HP) and 750 Nm (553 lb-ft) of torque it developed in the beginning made it the most powerful diesel passenger car on the planet, and this obviously weighed more than the potential reliability and maintenance problems its specific architecture also came with.
Audi Q7 V12 TDI: The Most Monstruous Passenger Car Diesel Engine in History Even compared with the ultra-intricate architecture of the gasoline W12, the V12 TDI stands tall as one of the most extreme engines ever fitted to a production road car. It is also one of the most in-your-face expressions of Ferdinand Piech’s personal conviction that excessive engineering can trump every other powertrain philosophy.
Apart from that, the Austrian also wanted to prove that the Volkswagen Group’s TDI badge was the most powerful diesel technology on the planet, so, once again, it needed a halo model. Following Audi’s 24 Hours of Le Mans successes using the TDI badge, Piech simply decided that there isn’t anything better to celebrate those victories than the world’s first (and so far last) V12 diesel.
Photo: Audi AG Initially, the 5.9-liter V12 TDI was supposed to power a version of the first-generation Audi R8 as well, and there was even a concept car, but the 2008 financial crisis and possible common sense kept Piech from giving it the go-ahead. Instead, the only twelve-cylinder passenger car diesel ever made was only offered on the first-generation Audi Q7.
Leaving the proprietary Pumpe Duse technology behind, the VW Group had already started switching to Common Rail technology by that time, so it wasn’t simply a case of taking the V10 TDI and adding two more cylinders at each bank’s end. Instead, the 5.9-liter V12 was actually created fusing two 3.0-liter V6s longitudinally, thus doubling their length. From this perspective, it was a much larger (and heavier) twelve cylinder than the gasoline W12, so it’s a wonder it even fit under the hood of the Audi Q7.
To squeeze the massive diesel powertrain into the Q7, Audi’s engineers had to completely redesign the model's front end, front axle, and cooling systems. The SUV was hand-assembled on a separate production line and came standard with massive 420mm carbon-ceramic brakes just to keep its massive 2.6-ton weight in check. It was never used on another car since, and its development costs were probably never recovered, but that only goes hand in hand with most of Ferdinand Piech’s quirky engine ideas.
